Uḍupi
(‘the place where चन्द्र [Moon] was blessed [by शिव]’)
------------------------------------------
Uḍupi is one of the most famous and popular places of पिल्ग्रिमगे, especially to the Vaiṣṇavas.
It is in the South Kanara district of the Karnataka State (in south India), situated on the seashore at a distance of 60 kms. (37 miles) to the north of the city of Mangalore.
Kṛṣṇa TempleCandra or the deity मोओन् (also called Uḍupa) is said to have performed austerities here to rid himself of the curse of दक्ष प्रजापति. He was redeemed by Lord शिव. A temple dedicated to Candramauḷīśvara (Śiva) is situated here now.
Another ancient temple is that of Ananteśvara, right opposite the चन्द्र-mauḷīśvara temple.
Both the temples belong to the period 7th to 9th century A. D.
Uḍupi—also called Rajatapīṭhapura—is now famous for its कृष्ण temple and the eight Maṭhas (monasteries) established by मध्वाचार्य (A.

-1317). The कृष्ण temple also was built by him after he secured the beautiful image from a big lump of yellow clay which had been used as a ballast by a ship. The ship was about to sink when मध्वाचार्य saved it by using his divine powers. He then obtained that heap of clay as a present at his own request. After recovering the image he carried it on his head to the present place and built the temple.
The image is that of child कृष्ण, in the standing posture, holding the churning rod in the left hand and a rope in the right. Sculptured out of the शालग्राम stone (by the divine architect विश्वकर्म himself) and worshipped by रुक्मिणी, it was later secured by अर्जुन (the Pāṇḍava hero) who hid it in clay before his departure. This is how the local legends describe the origin of the image.
It is 38 cms. (15 inches) in height.
The temple, built of black granite stone, is rather a small structure. To the right of the main entrance is the Madhvasarovara, the temple tank. The main entrance gate is facing north whereas the deity is facing west. It can be seen only through a small open window, known as ‘Kanakana kiṇḍi’ (‘Kanaka’s Window’). When कनकदास (A.

-1606), the famous devotee of कृष्ण was denied entrance into the temple because he belonged to a low caste, he prayed to the Lord with an intensely yearning heart for darśan. In response to his prayer, कृष्ण’s image turned towards the west where कनकदास was standing and an opening appeared on the wall mysteriously, thus enabling him to see the Lord.
The main festivals of the Śrī कृष्ण temple are: Saptotsava (a seven-day festival celebrated during the middle of January), Madhvanavamī (the day on which मध्वाचार्य disappeared from the world), Śrī कृष्ण Jayantī (birthday of Lord Śrī कृष्ण in August-September), Lakṣa-dīpotsava (on the day of उत्थानद्वादशी generally in November), and Paryāya-mahotsava.
The pontiffs of each of the eight maṭhas (monasteries) got a two-month term to worship the image of कृष्ण in the temple. Since this was considered too short a period, वादिराज (A.

-1600), the best of the pontiffs at that time, raised it to two years. So, there is a change of guard—the next pontiff taking over the responsibility of running the कृष्ण temple —every two years, during the last part of January. This is called पर्यायमहोत्सव.
Other festivals are: रामनवमी, Narasiṁhajayantī, Anantacaturdaśī, मकर-सङ्क्रान्ति and दीपावली.
A few more holy places around उडुपि worth visiting are: Ambalapāḍi (with an ancient temple of Janārdana as also of Mahākālī); Daṇḍatīrtha (a tank built by मध्वाचार्य); Nadyantādi (where there is a मठ as also two bathing places called Gadātīrtha and Gautamakuṇḍa) and Kaḍtila or Setutila (where मध्वाचार्य established the image of Gopālakṛṣṇa).
See also MADHVĀCĀRYA and KANAKA-DĀSA.
